patient.name: Eleanor Matsumoto
patient.chief_complaint: Three-year progressive bilateral foot burning and numbness, poorly controlled diabetes
patient.hpi: Eleanor Matsumoto is a 59-year-old retired secretary with a 3-year history of bilateral foot burning, tingling, and numbness in the context of longstanding poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. She describes a constant burning sensation in both feet described as 'walking on hot coals,' worse at night, and notes numbness progressing from the toes to mid-foot. She has also developed bilateral lower leg numbness over the past year. She has had multiple diabetes-related complications: background diabetic retinopathy diagnosed 18 months ago requiring laser photocoagulation, and microalbuminuria identified 2 years ago. Her diabetes has been poorly controlled for over a decade — she has had HbA1c values ranging from 9-11% for years, with current HbA1c of 10.8%. She has been non-adherent with both diet and medications, attributing this to caring for her elderly mother. She denies alcohol use. She reports her feet have become numb enough that she burned the sole of her left foot on a hot bath mat last month without noticing it for several hours — she is alarmed by this sensory loss. Her primary care physician referred her after noting absent ankle reflexes and a foot ulcer scar on the left plantar surface.
pmh: Diabetic retinopathy (background, treated with laser photocoagulation)
patient.review_of_systems: Positive: bilateral foot burning and numbness, diabetic retinopathy, microalbuminuria, left plantar burn injury (painless). Negative: weakness, falls, ataxia, hand symptoms, bowel/bladder dysfunction.

report.summary: SEVERELY ABNORMAL NCS/EMG. LENGTH-DEPENDENT AXONAL SENSORIMOTOR POLYNEUROPATHY — classic diabetic pattern. Absent SNAPs bilaterally (lower > upper extremity). Reduced motor amplitudes with relatively preserved but mildly slow velocities. EMG shows chronic denervation in distal muscles.

motor.flag: markedly reduced amplitude; mildly slow velocity — axonal loss

sensory.flag: mildly reduced amplitude — length-dependent, upper extremity relatively spared

sensory.nerve: Right Sural Sensory (note: could also test plantar)

muscles_tested.morphology: mildly polyphasic — minimal upper extremity involvement

emg.summary: Distal > proximal denervation consistent with length-dependent diabetic axonal neuropathy.

report.overall_impression: LENGTH-DEPENDENT AXONAL SENSORIMOTOR POLYNEUROPATHY. Absent sural and superficial peroneal SNAPs. Markedly reduced peroneal and tibial motor amplitudes. Relatively preserved upper extremity NCS. Classic diabetic polyneuropathy pattern. Severity correlates with duration of poor glycemic control (HbA1c 10.8%).

report.summary: QSART bilateral feet: absent (0 uL). Bilateral legs: severely reduced (0.08 uL). HRV: markedly reduced vagal modulation. Orthostatic vitals: BP 148/92 supine → 118/72 at 3 min standing → 112/68 at 5 min — significant orthostatic hypotension (30/20 mmHg drop — meets diagnostic criteria). Diabetic cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy confirmed. Increased risk of cardiovascular events and silent MI.
report.interpretation: Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN) in advanced diabetic neuropathy. Orthostatic hypotension must be managed (compression stockings, salt/water, midodrine if needed). CAN increases cardiac event risk 3-fold.

report.summary: Diabetic foot assessment: Bilateral absent monofilament sensation (5.07 Semmes-Weinstein). Absent vibration bilateral feet. Left plantar scar (healed ulcer). Callus right great toe — pre-ulcerative. Bilateral dry skin (autonomic insufficiency). Peripheral vascular assessment: ABI right 0.82 (borderline, mild peripheral arterial disease), left 0.88. Doppler: Biphasic signals bilateral posterior tibials and dorsalis pedis — adequate perfusion for healing.
report.recommendations: HIGH-RISK DIABETIC FOOT. Monthly podiatry visits. Therapeutic footwear (custom molded orthotics — Medicare coverage for diabetic foot). Daily foot inspection education. Avoid barefoot walking. Debride right great toe callus. Refer vascular surgery if ABI drops below 0.7.
report.interpretation: High-risk foot with prior ulcer history, absent monofilament, and borderline PAD. Without intensive management, annual re-ulceration risk is >50%. Therapeutic footwear and regular podiatry essential.

output.query: duloxetine pregabalin diabetic neuropathic pain treatment guidelines

results.citation: AAN Guideline 2011: Treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy. Neurology 76:1758-1765.
results.summary: Duloxetine 60 mg/day: Level A evidence for PDPN. Pregabalin 300-600 mg/day: Level A evidence. Gabapentin 900-3600 mg/day: Level B. TCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline): Level B, avoid in elderly and cardiac disease. Opioids: avoid unless refractory to first-line. Topical capsaicin 8% patch: Level B.

output.interpretation: Duloxetine 60 mg daily is first-line for painful diabetic polyneuropathy (Level A evidence, FDA-approved for DPNP). Given CKD stage 3b (eGFR 42), duloxetine dose adjustment is not strictly required but monitor. Pregabalin is an alternative but requires dose reduction in CKD (start 25 mg twice daily given eGFR 42). Current gabapentin 600 mg TID may need upward titration. Recommendation: switch to duloxetine as primary agent; reduce pregabalin/gabapentin if CNS side effects.

critical_actions: Podiatry referral with high-risk diabetic foot protocol — prior ulcer history + absent monofilament = imminent re-ulceration risk
Diabetes intensification — HbA1c 10.8% must be addressed to prevent neuropathy progression
Supplement B12 in all metformin-treated patients with low-normal B12
Autonomic testing — cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy increases cardiac event risk
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe NSAIDs for neuropathic pain — CKD stage 3b, will worsen renal function
Do not prescribe tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline) as first-line — CKD reduces clearance; cardiac risk
Do not prescribe pregabalin without dose reduction — CKD requires dose adjustment (25 mg BID for eGFR 42)

differential.key_distinguishing: B12 218 pg/mL low-normal from metformin; MMA only borderline; length-dependent NCS pattern is diabetic not B12 SCDC; B12 supplementation reasonable but not primary diagnosis
HbA1c 10.8% with 14-year diabetes and multiple complications provides overwhelming diabetic etiology; NCS pattern is axonal (length-dependent), not demyelinating; CSF not elevated
CKD stage 3b (eGFR 42) can contribute axonal neuropathy; however diabetes is the primary cause given 14-year history and retinopathy/nephropathy triad

key_reasoning_points: STRAIGHTFORWARD: Classic presentation of severe diabetic neuropathy with all expected features — poor glycemic control, multiple microvascular complications, length-dependent NCS, absent ankle reflexes, prior ulcer
REAL-SEEDED VARIATION: Based on published PMC case reports of DPNP with multiple complications — retinopathy + nephropathy + neuropathy triad is highly characteristic
HIGH-RISK FOOT: The combination of absent monofilament + prior ulcer history + dry skin (autonomic) + borderline PAD requires intensive preventive podiatric care
METFORMIN AND B12: Annual B12 monitoring is ADA recommended for metformin-treated patients; this commonly co-existing deficiency should be supplemented but not attributed as primary cause
